Text That Moves, Scripts That Pull

Two questions, both answered by measurement rather than by reading about it. What do the best explainers put on screen as type, and how do they animate and time it? And how do their scripts build and release tension, compared with ours? Frames sampled every half second from Half as Interesting, Vox and Johnny Harris; transcripts of five references counted word by word against our two scripts.

Part one. Text on screen

Three channels, three different answers, and the difference is the first finding: how much type is on screen is a channel decision, not a law. Half as Interesting puts a word on roughly half of all frames. Johnny Harris puts almost none on in his first three minutes; his text lives in books, maps and screens he is physically holding. Vox puts text on screen mostly as documents: real headlines and chart titles with a highlighter over the operative words.

The rules the frames agree on

A keyword, not a caption. One to four words: the noun, the number, the name or the date just spoken. Never the sentence. Half as Interesting's longest overlays are quotations, and those are typeset as quotations, not as subtitles.
On the word, through the phrase, off on the cut. Type lands within a frame or two of the word and stays while the phrase runs, 1.5 to 6 seconds, then leaves with the cut rather than fading on its own clock.
Build, do not replace. A list accretes: each new item pops beside the last. A phrase grows word by word. A correction happens in place. Replacing text on every beat is what reads as frantic.
One face, one colour, one stroke. The whole channel uses the same type treatment on footage. The variety is in what the words say and where they land, not in fonts and colours.
Documents get a highlighter. Real pages are shown as themselves; the only added type is a swept highlight over the words being read, and sometimes an arrow. This is what we already do in the document scenes.
The type can be the turn. A question mark alone. A word crossed out. A number that changes. A misspelling underlined. When the argument turns, the type turns with it, which is where "tension" and "kinetic text" meet.

Part two. Tension in the script

Same yardstick for everyone: counts per hundred words from the transcripts, so a 21-minute film and a 3-minute one compare. "Turns" are the words that pivot an argument: but, however, until, instead, turns out, the problem, the catch. "Stakes" are the words that make it the viewer's business: you, everyone, nobody, every, never, the most, the only, the first, the last.

What the counts say

  • Questions are level. Ours ask as often as theirs. That is not the gap.
  • Turns are half. They pivot the argument two to three times a minute; we do it about once. Our scripts state; theirs state, then contradict, then resolve. This is the "but, therefore" rule in the numbers: between two beats a story needs a but or a therefore, never an and then. Our paragraph joins are mostly and then.
  • Numbers are three to ten times denser in ours. Figures are our strength and also why the videos can feel like a ledger. The pros spend a number when it lands a turn, not on every line.
  • There is no narrator. First person is zero in both of ours. Harris is at 3.2 per hundred words, WSJ 1.9, Vox 1.2. "Here is the part that surprised me" was the one line of ours with a person in it, and it is the line you liked.
  • Our hooks have no question and no turn. Every reference except Harris opens with two to four questions inside 20 seconds; Search Party opens with three turns. Ours open with a claim and a number.
  • Promises are rare everywhere. "In this video", "here's what you need to know": near zero across the set. The pros do not announce the payoff; they withhold it.

The doctrine behind the counts

  • But, therefore. Outline the video as beats. Between each pair write the connector. If it is "and then", cut or rewrite the beat. Conflict (but) and consequence (therefore) are the only two joins a story tolerates.
  • The hook does three jobs in 15 seconds: immediate relevance to the viewer, a curiosity gap, and a concrete expectation of value. First line under twelve words. No throat-clearing. The hook may promise only what the video delivers. Most viewers decide in about eight seconds; more than half are gone by sixty.
  • Setup, tension, payoff, in loops. Long-form runs five to seven loops; a two-minute piece has room for two or three. Each setup names what the segment answers and what it costs to ignore; the tension teaches without revealing; the payoff gives the concrete answer and connects it to the next question. Write the payoffs first.
  • Open loops, planted and paid. A question or mystery every 45 to 60 seconds that is not resolved until later, and never a resolution without the next tease. A re-hook at 60 to 70 percent of the runtime.
  • Stakes density and no dead air. The MrBeast doctrine, stripped of its surface: re-hook every 20 to 40 seconds, raise the stakes, know what minute mark you are at, end abruptly after the payoff.
  • Tension in the picture and the sound. The slow push before a reveal; the hold on a document before the highlight; the count-up; the music bed cut a beat before the number lands, so the figure arrives in silence; the dark ground. Cut the video with no music first and mark where it breathes.

Part three. The 2026 uploads

The owner's objection to parts one and two was fair: four of the seven references were 2018 to 2024. So the same measurements were run again on eight uploads from February to August 2026 (Search Party, PolyMatter, Wendover, Half as Interesting, Cleo Abram, Johnny Harris, Economics Explained, Vox), and four of them were framed every half second for their first thirty seconds. Three things changed, and one did not.

What changed since the older set

  • The hook is a scene, not a question. Seven of eight open on a place and a date or a named person, with no title and no "in this video". Questions come after the scene. The first turn ("but", "except") lands inside twenty seconds, and in every framed case it comes with a visual change: map to news footage, aircraft to lawsuit paper.
  • Turns went up. 0.78 to 1.53 per hundred words against 0.69 to 1.07 in the older set. The argument pivots more often than it did.
  • Type got quieter and more precise. Half as Interesting's yellow capitals on every shot are gone; 2026 HAI is mixed case, fewer words, on flat brand grounds. What replaced the wall of words is three devices, and all four framed videos use at least one.
  • What did not change: first person is still everywhere but ours (0.5 to 4.1), promises are still near zero, and numbers are still spent, not sprayed (0.8 to 4.4 per hundred words).

The three type devices of 2026, now in our pipeline

  • The dated slug. Small, top-left, stamped over the opening scene: *@May 7, 2025.*
  • One giant word for the turn. *!Nobody voted to end it.* fills the width once, where the argument pivots.
  • The label that swaps in place. *=skiplagging* flips out the item before it, for a thing being renamed or a figure being corrected.

What this means for the two videos we have

Penny and REAL ID are figure-dense and turn-poor. Both hooks are statements. Both have exactly one question in the body. Neither pays an open loop with a reveal that was withheld; the figures arrive as soon as they are named. Neither has a narrator. And the type on screen, outside the cards and documents, is four or five figures per video where Half as Interesting would put forty.

What changes, in order

  1. A keyword layer. Mark words in the script with asterisks (*3.69 cents*) and every figure, date and agency name gets marked automatically. Each lands on its word in one house treatment, holds through the phrase, leaves on the cut. Lists accrete beside each other (the REAL ID deadlines: 2011, 2013, 2020, 2021, 2023 stacking up as they are spoken). Quotations are typeset as quotations, phrase by phrase. Target: type on about four in ten footage shots.
  2. A script check before the voice. Turns per hundred words at or above 0.8; a question inside the first 20 seconds; first line under twelve words; one open loop planted in the first 20 seconds and paid after the 60 percent mark; a connector test at every paragraph join that flags "and then"; one line of first person per chapter. The check prints the failures; the human rewrites.
  3. Withhold the figure. When a number is the payoff, the sentence before it names the question and the card lands a beat after the word, with the bed cut for that beat. The 3.69 cents line was written this way and is the moment that works.
  4. Type that turns. A question mark alone on the cut before a reveal; a crossed-out figure when a claim is corrected; a number that changes in place. Three templates, used sparingly, only where the argument turns.
  5. Sound for tension. A low riser under the setup line of each loop, a bed drop on the payoff, a tick on every keyword pop.

Limits

Auto-captions carry no punctuation, so "question" is counted by question words, which also catches "what it costs"; the same proxy was applied to our scripts so the comparison is fair, and it is a proxy. Text density is my count from frames sampled every three seconds, not a frame-by-frame measure. Animation curves cannot be read from stills: what I can say is when type appears and disappears, not how it moves in between. Half as Interesting is a comedy channel and Harris is a personality channel; neither is our shape, and the rules above are the ones all three agree on.
